strengths: The paper tackles an important problem and presents a simple, scalable combination of class-conditional feature prototypes and per-class BatchNorm regularization. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-k2n5upce/call-89d9f90ed444432a8272aa70064bc34f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reported classification results are strong: WMDD leads the compared methods in most ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K settings, and its 100-IPC results approach the paper's full-data references.

The evaluation is broader than a single benchmark result. It includes multiple image budgets, five evaluation architectures, runtime and memory measurements, component ablations, an alternative sliced-Wasserstein variant, hyperparameter sensitivity, and qualitative inspection.

Table 4 provides repeated-run evidence that both PCBN and barycenter-feature matching contribute. The gains of Wasserstein matching over the CE counterpart under PCBN are modest but consistent across all three datasets.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, provides algorithms and principal hyperparameters, appropriately cites the inherited SRe2L and optimal-transport machinery, links code, and acknowledges bias propagation in its societal-impact discussion.
weaknesses: The central novelty is overstated. With one input distribution, squared Euclidean cost, freely optimized support locations, and free weights, Eqs. 5-11 reduce to classical optimal quantization/k-means: eliminating the weights makes the objective the average squared distance to the nearest prototype, and Eq. 11 is the cluster-mean update. The paper neither explains this equivalence nor compares against a standard feature-space k-means/prototype baseline. Figure 2's barycenter of multiple distributions therefore does not closely represent the actual N=1 procedure.

Attribution of the headline gains to Wasserstein geometry is not convincing. In Table 4, replacing CE with the Wasserstein target under PCBN adds only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 points at 10 IPC, while PCBN and other pipeline choices account for much of the improvement. Moreover, the internal CE+BN result reaches 35.9% on ImageNet-1K, far above the 21.3% reported for SRe2L in Table 1, indicating that mixing literature numbers with the authors' stronger implementation substantially exaggerates the apparent advantage. Controlled reruns of the closest baselines across all budgets are needed.

The MMD comparison does not isolate the metric: Figure 4 compares different algorithmic frameworks and encoders, while the claimed direct MMD replacement is not fully specified or tabulated. In particular, at one support point the proposed W2 quantizer targets the feature mean, closely connecting it to linear-kernel mean matching, which makes the large 1-IPC difference especially difficult to attribute to Wasserstein geometry alone.

The supplementary theory studies W1, whereas the implemented objective uses squared Euclidean transport, i.e. W2 squared. Its Wasserstein and MMD bounds contain incomparable constants and do not establish superiority. The Hessian derivation also treats the optimal transport plan as fixed even though it changes with the support positions, so the description as a classical Newton step and the unqualified convergence claim require correction.

Important reproducibility and efficiency details remain unclear, including barycenter initialization, the projected-subgradient step size, handling of zero weights, the exact use of learned weights during FKD/evaluation, augmentation and evaluation schedules, and hyperparameter-selection data. Table 3 also does not clearly state whether teacher training, feature extraction, barycenter computation, and relabeling are all included in the reported end-to-end cost.

The experimental scope is limited to classification datasets closely related to ImageNet, and the qualitative t-SNE study uses an embedding model trained on a mixture containing the evaluated synthetic samples. No nearest-neighbor or leakage analysis is supplied despite the privacy motivation and natural-looking reconstructions. These limitations temper the breadth and societal claims.

strengths: The paper addresses the important problem of scalable dataset distillation with a simple, interpretable combination of classwise feature representatives and per-class BatchNorm regularization.

The empirical results are strong and broad. WMDD achieves substantial gains on Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-1K, particularly at higher IPC budgets, and approaches the reported full-data ResNet-18 accuracy.
Cross-architecture experiments covering larger ResNets and ViTs provide useful evidence that the distilled data are not narrowly overfit to the ResNet-18 distillation architecture.

The evaluation includes component ablations, comparison with sliced Wasserstein distance, hyperparameter and feature-layer studies, runtime and memory measurements, qualitative diversity analysis, three-run statistics for the main results, implementation details, and a public-code link.
weaknesses: With one input distribution and freely optimized support locations and masses, Eq. (5)'s squared-Wasserstein problem reduces to classical vector quantization/k-means. The paper neither discusses this equivalence nor provides the essential feature-space k-means baseline, weakening the claimed Wasserstein-specific originality.

The experiments do not fully isolate the Wasserstein contribution. Table 4 changes the feature objective rather than only the distribution metric, while the MMD comparison uses a different algorithmic framework. Comparisons using the same teacher features, optimization budget, PCBN, and characteristic-kernel MMD—as well as uniform-weight and k-means controls—are needed.

The supplementary theory concerns a generic W1 Lipschitz bound, whereas the implemented method uses squared Euclidean costs corresponding to W2. It does not establish superiority over MMD. Moreover, the stated Hessian and Newton interpretation treat the optimal transport plan as fixed despite its dependence on the support positions, so the convergence claim needs qualification.

Most headline baseline values are imported from prior papers, making exact protocol comparability uncertain. The efficiency study is limited to ImageNette and does not clearly account for teacher training, full-data feature/statistics extraction, barycenter construction, and FKD. Important reproducibility details such as barycenter initialization, the weight-update learning rate, zero-weight handling, and precise use of learned masses during evaluation are also omitted.

strengths: WMDD is a simple, computationally attractive pipeline combining classwise feature prototypes, feature inversion, and per-class BatchNorm regularization without differentiating through model training.

The empirical coverage is strong: ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K are evaluated at several IPC budgets, with substantial reported gains in many large-scale settings, including 57.6% at 50 IPC and 60.7% at 100 IPC on ImageNet-1K.
The paper includes useful cross-architecture tests, runtime and memory measurements, a sliced-Wasserstein comparison, hyperparameter and layer sensitivity studies, and qualitative diversity analyses.
The factorial ablation of feature loss and PCBN usefully shows that PCBN is an effective component. Hyperparameters, pseudocode, dataset attribution, and a public code link also aid reproducibility.
The presentation is generally clear, and the supplementary discussion appropriately acknowledges that distillation may preserve source-data biases.
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing substantially overstates the novelty. Equation (5) is a one-input, support-constrained Wasserstein approximation, not a conventional multi-distribution barycenter. With free weights and squared Euclidean cost, eliminating the transport weights yields the standard vector-quantization/k-means objective. The paper neither recognizes this equivalence nor compares against classwise k-means, feature clustering, or related coreset baselines.

The optimization derivation is not fully sound as written. Because the transport plan changes with the support positions, the minimized Wasserstein objective is generally nonsmooth and does not globally have Hessian 2wjI. Equation (11) is defensible as an update conditional on a fixed transport plan, but not as the stated Newton step on the complete objective; the claimed convergence to a local optimum is unsupported.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of the Wasserstein component. With PCBN fixed, Table 4 shows only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 percentage-point improvements over cross-entropy on the three datasets, whereas PCBN accounts for much larger changes. Figure 4 compares different algorithmic pipelines after selectively removing components rather than substituting MMD and Wasserstein within a controlled common pipeline.

The theoretical appendix does not establish superiority over MMD: it analyzes W1 although the method uses squared Euclidean W2 transport, presents two bounds with incomparable unknown constants, and then criticizes only practical linear-kernel mean matching rather than MMD generally. It also does not address the poor high-dimensional sample complexity associated with Wasserstein estimation.

Table 1 mixes reported baseline numbers with newly run results while asserting identical settings without documenting protocol equivalence. Several comparisons lack uncertainty estimates, and the cross-architecture experiment reports no variability and uses an insufficiently specified 20% synthetic holdout procedure.

Important reproducibility and efficiency details remain unspecified, including support initialization, the projected-subgradient learning rate, feature normalization, safeguards for zero learned weights, and precisely how weights enter FKD/student training. Efficiency is measured only on ImageNette at 1 IPC, without an ImageNet-scale end-to-end accounting of teacher training, full-data feature/statistics extraction, relabeling, and label-storage overhead.

strengths: The method targets an important problem and offers a simple, scalable combination of class-wise feature summarization, synthetic-image inversion, and per-class BatchNorm regularization. The presentation is generally clear and the synthetic images are qualitatively compelling. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xdmtp6az/call-09f6d243450142d2921d131f5e5c9ae9/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reported large-scale results are strong. On ImageNet-1K, WMDD obtains 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% at 10, 50, and 100 IPC, respectively, exceeding every comparator reported in Table 1; the gains on Tiny-ImageNet are also substantial.
Cross-architecture evaluation covers three ResNets and two ViTs, with WMDD performing best throughout Table 2. The runtime and memory results also suggest recovery is nearly as efficient as SRe2L.

The paper includes component ablations, comparisons with MMD and sliced Wasserstein variants, hyperparameter and layer sensitivity, multiple-run error estimates for its main results, public code, and a reasonable discussion of bias and environmental impact.
weaknesses: The central mathematical construction is insufficiently distinguished from standard vector quantization. With one target distribution, freely learned masses, and squared Euclidean ground cost, Eq. 5 reduces after eliminating the transport weights to (1/n) sum_i min_j ||x_i-b_j||^2—ordinary class-wise k-means in teacher-feature space. Calling this a Wasserstein barycenter, using a multi-distribution barycenter example in Fig. 2, and omitting discussion or attribution of the k-means equivalence materially weaken the originality claim. A direct feature-k-means/deep-inversion baseline is essential.

The experiments do not cleanly attribute the headline gains to Wasserstein matching. In Table 4, the same-pipeline CE+BN baseline reaches 35.9% on ImageNet-1K at 10 IPC, far above the 21.3% reported for SRe2L in Table 1; WMDD reaches 38.1%, or only 2.2 points more. CE+PCBN reaches 36.4%. Comparable controlled baselines are absent at 50 and 100 IPC, while the MMD comparison in Fig. 4 uses heavily stripped-down pipelines whose accuracies are far below the complete method.

The supplementary theory analyzes W1, whereas the implemented algorithm uses squared Euclidean cost corresponding to W2 squared. It presents two standard expected-loss bounds under different, unquantified assumptions and constants; it neither establishes superiority over MMD nor connects adequately to teacher-feature matching, imperfect feature inversion, or training a new classifier.

Some optimization claims need greater rigor. The stated Hessian treats the optimal transport plan as fixed although it changes with support positions, the claimed convergence to a local optimum is unsupported, and projected updates may produce zero masses for which the position update divides by zero. Initialization, barycenter step size, projection details, and the precise use of learned weights during FKD are not specified in the manuscript, although released code partly mitigates reproducibility concerns.

Most baseline numbers are imported rather than reproduced under a unified pipeline, cross-architecture results lack uncertainty estimates, and efficiency is measured only on ImageNette at 1 IPC without clearly accounting for teacher training. Thus, despite strong empirical promise, the evidence and framing leave a slight balance toward rejection until the simple-quantization equivalence and fair in-pipeline comparisons are addressed.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-exg8_nsb/call-4d8f6526b6e144b0a405c0a6a104cd0d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem and reports strong results on three high-resolution benchmarks. WMDD reaches 60.7% on ImageNet-1K at 100 IPC, compared with 57.9% for the strongest listed baseline, and performs especially well at moderate and large IPC.

The combination of feature prototypes, learned sample weights, inversion through a pretrained classifier, and per-class BatchNorm regularization is simple and practically useful. Table 4 shows that PCBN consistently improves results across all three datasets.

The evaluation is broad: multiple IPC budgets, ResNet-to-ResNet/ViT transfer, runtime and memory, component ablations, sliced Wasserstein comparison, layer and regularization sensitivity, and qualitative diversity analyses. Main results include variability over repeated runs.

The presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The paper cites the datasets, POT implementation, and inherited distillation pipeline; supplies substantial implementation details and public code; and discusses bias and environmental impact.
weaknesses: The central formulation has a major unaddressed equivalence. With one input distribution and freely optimized support weights, Eqs. 5-8 reduce under squared Euclidean cost to feature-space vector quantization/k-means: eliminating the free weights lets every real point send its mass to its nearest prototype, while Eq. 11 updates each prototype to its cluster centroid. The paper neither acknowledges this degeneration of the claimed barycenter nor compares against or appropriately discusses a simple k-means baseline, substantially weakening originality and attribution of the gains to optimal transport.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the Wasserstein contribution. Table 4 compares Wasserstein feature matching with cross-entropy, not with k-means or a controlled MMD objective; moreover, Wasserstein with ordinary BN is worse than CE with ordinary BN on Tiny ImageNet (36.6 vs. 38.0) and ImageNet-1K (26.8 vs. 35.9). Figure 4 compares broader method configurations after changing/removing pipeline components. Uniform-weight, learned-weight, PCBN-only, and simple clustered-prototype controls are missing.

The theoretical appendix gives standard expected-loss bounds for W1 and MMD but the implemented objective uses squared W2 in pretrained feature space. Neither the unknown Lipschitz/RKHS constants nor the resulting bounds are compared, so the analysis establishes no advantage for WMDD. Its discussion of quadratic MMD cost also omits common sampling and kernel-approximation alternatives.

Baseline comparability and efficiency evidence are incomplete. Table 1 mostly combines reported results without fully establishing identical training, augmentation, or model-selection protocols; Table 2 lacks uncertainty estimates. Table 3 covers only 1-IPC ImageNette and excludes the strongest recent baselines, while no end-to-end ImageNet-1K runtime including teacher pretraining, barycenter computation, and FKD is reported despite the scalability claim.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified in the manuscript: prototype initialization, projected-subgradient step size, treatment of zero weights in the 1/w update, and exactly how learned weights enter FKD training. Several later-stage settings are delegated wholesale to SRe2L. The released code mitigates this concern but does not make the paper self-contained.

The reported large-scale results are strong: WMDD improves substantially over the listed methods on Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-1K at 10–100 IPC, with results averaged over three runs and uncertainty reported for the main experiments.

The evaluation is broader than a single benchmark result, including ResNet-to-ResNet and ResNet-to-ViT transfer, component ablations, regularization and layer sensitivity, a sliced-Wasserstein comparison, resource measurements, and qualitative inspection of synthetic-image diversity.
Public code is provided, and the supplement documents the main optimization settings, hardware, algorithms, and a reasonable societal-impact discussion acknowledging inherited dataset bias.
weaknesses: The central formulation is conceptually overstated. With one input distribution, freely learned weights, an at-most-m-point support, and squared Euclidean transport cost, Eq. (5) is essentially optimal vector quantization/k-means in pretrained feature space—not a Wasserstein barycenter in the usual multi-distribution sense. Figure 2 therefore does not directly motivate the actual algorithm. The paper neither explains this equivalence nor compares against feature k-means, medoids, or other prototype-selection baselines; moreover, image recovery in Eq. (12) is ordinary pointwise L2 feature matching rather than Wasserstein matching.

The evidence isolating the Wasserstein contribution is insufficient. The MMD comparison uses a fundamentally different method and feature setup, removes augmentations and FKD, and does not present a controlled implementation using a well-tuned characteristic kernel. Table 4 instead compares the proposed targets with cross-entropy targets, conflating the metric, target construction, and learned weights.

There is a serious unexplained baseline inconsistency: CE+BN obtains 35.9% on ImageNet-1K at 10 IPC in Table 4, whereas SRe2L—described as the corresponding prior CE+BN design—has 21.3% in Table 1. Because Table 1 largely mixes externally reported numbers with the authors' results, this 14.6-point discrepancy undermines the claimed margin and the assertion of identical settings.

The theoretical appendix does not justify superiority over MMD. It gives standard integral-probability-metric bounds with incomparable, uncontrolled constants and assumptions, and analyzes W1 although the implemented objective and Newton updates use squared W2. The derivation also treats the transport plan as locally fixed when presenting the Hessian, without addressing nonsmooth assignment changes, zero-weight supports, or convergence of the alternating procedure.

The scalability evidence is incomplete. Table 3 measures ImageNette only at 1 IPC, where the transport problem is effectively trivial, and reports GPU memory without host memory or a breakdown of feature extraction, barycenter computation, teacher training, and FKD. End-to-end ImageNet-1K time, memory, and total storage—including soft labels and weights—are absent.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified despite the code link: barycenter-support initialization, subgradient learning rate and schedule, projection and empty-support handling, exact optimal-transport solver settings, and precisely how learned weights enter FKD/student training. Cross-architecture results and several secondary experiments also lack uncertainty estimates.

The claim of approaching full-data performance is overstated for ImageNet-1K: the cited full-data ResNet-18 reaches only 63.1%, substantially below standard ResNet-18 ImageNet performance. The unusual 20% synthetic-data holdout used for cross-architecture model selection and the qualitative t-SNE/diversity evidence further require stronger justification or quantitative validation.

strengths: The paper addresses the important practical problem of scaling dataset distillation to high-resolution data with a conceptually simple feature-prototype and per-class BatchNorm pipeline.

Table 1 reports strong results on ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K, including 60.7% ImageNet-1K accuracy at 100 IPC versus 63.1% for full-data training. Results include repeated runs and uncertainty estimates.

The evaluation covers useful dimensions beyond headline accuracy: cross-architecture transfer, runtime and memory, component ablations, sliced-Wasserstein comparison, hyperparameter sensitivity, feature-layer choice, and qualitative diversity.
The authors cite the inherited SRe2L/FKD machinery and optimal-transport implementation, provide a code link and several implementation settings, and acknowledge inherited dataset bias.
weaknesses: The central novelty is substantially overstated. Equation 5 uses a single input distribution, so this is not a nontrivial multi-distribution Wasserstein barycenter. With freely optimized weights and squared Euclidean cost, minimizing the Wasserstein distance to an at-most-m-atom measure reduces to standard feature-space quantization—the k-means objective. The paper neither discusses this equivalence nor compares against or appropriately situates a k-means/quantization baseline.

The experiments do not convincingly isolate a benefit from the Wasserstein metric. Under PCBN, replacing the proposed loss with cross-entropy changes 10-IPC accuracy by only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 points on the three datasets in Table 4; without PCBN, Wasserstein is substantially worse on Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-1K. Both ablation branches also appear to retain transport-derived weights, so this is not a clean removal of the OT component.

The MMD comparison is not controlled: Figure 4 compares different algorithmic frameworks after selectively removing engineering components, while the claimed near-random result from directly substituting MMD is not numerically reported or diagnosed. Consequently, the evidence does not support broad claims that Wasserstein geometry explains the gains.

The supplementary theory analyzes a W1 generalization bound, whereas the implemented squared-Euclidean transport objective is W2-squared. MMD receives an analogous bound, and the paper neither estimates the incomparable constants nor derives a result showing a tighter downstream-error guarantee. The discussion therefore does not establish the asserted superiority.

The optimization justification is incomplete. The stated Hessian treats the optimal transport plan as fixed even though it changes with the support, so the value function is generally nonsmooth and the update is not a conventional Newton step. Moreover, Algorithm 2 updates weights after computing the transport plan and then reuses that plan for the position update, creating ambiguity about which marginal constraints and Hessian are valid. The claimed convergence to a local optimum is unsupported.

Comparison fairness is insufficiently documented. Most Table 1 baselines are copied from prior papers rather than rerun in one protocol, despite the claim of identical settings. The large gap between SRe2L and the CE-plus-standard-BN ablation is unexplained; cross-architecture results lack uncertainty; and efficiency is assessed primarily on the small 10-class ImageNette setting without clearly itemizing teacher training, feature extraction, barycenter computation, FKD, and evaluation costs.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: the manuscript omits prototype initialization, the transport weight learning rate and schedule, solver details, precise use of learned weights during FKD/training, augmentation settings, and full evaluation schedules. Referring generally to SRe2L does not make the method self-contained.

Qualitative images and t-SNE plots are suggestive but do not quantitatively validate improved diversity or distribution coverage. The paper also does not study dependence on the teacher architecture, tasks beyond classification, privacy leakage, or end-to-end energy use, limiting several broader impact claims.

strengths: WMDD is a simple, practically relevant approach that combines feature-space distribution summarization with per-class BatchNorm regularization and scales to high-resolution data. The method is clearly presented with algorithms and implementation settings. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-q7h0jhxr/call-5d08ac892b4a4c16a964b4b259cb0efe/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical results are strong, particularly at moderate and large budgets: WMDD reports 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% on ImageNet-1K at 10, 50, and 100 IPC, respectively, outperforming the cited results of several recent scalable methods.

The evaluation is broader than is typical for large-scale dataset distillation: it covers three datasets, four IPC budgets, cross-architecture transfer to ResNets and ViTs, runtime and memory, component ablations, layer and regularization sensitivity, and comparison with sliced Wasserstein distance.

The synthesized ImageNet images are recognizable and qualitatively more varied than the displayed SRe2L samples. Reporting multiple-run uncertainty for the principal results, citing the datasets and software, providing a code link, and discussing potential bias and energy impact are also positive.
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing is problematic. Equation 5 uses one source distribution and an at-most-m-atom target with freely optimized weights. Eliminating the weights and transport plan reduces this W2-squared objective to ordinary feature-space vector quantization: each real feature is assigned to its nearest support, the supports become cluster means, and their weights are cluster proportions. Thus this is not a Wasserstein barycenter in the usual multi-distribution sense; with N=1 the unconstrained barycenter is simply the original distribution. The absence of a k-means/vector-quantization baseline and related attribution makes it impossible to establish that optimal transport, rather than feature clustering plus inversion, is the source of the gains.

The optimization analysis overstates its guarantees. The claimed Hessian 2 w_j I and exact Newton update treat the optimal transport plan as fixed even though it changes with the support locations; the value function is only piecewise smooth. No proof is given for the asserted convergence of the alternating support-and-weight procedure to a local optimum.

The theoretical appendix does not substantiate the method or its claimed advantage over MMD. It gives standard bounds for W1 while the implemented objective uses squared Euclidean cost/W2-squared, and it never compares the unknown Lipschitz and RKHS constants. Its discussion of MMD mainly contrasts against linear-kernel mean matching and claims quadratic cost, although constant real-real terms or approximations can avoid that cost. Consequently, it establishes no ordering between the metrics.

The headline baseline comparison is insufficiently controlled because nearly all competing numbers are copied from prior papers. Most notably, the manuscript's own CE+BN control obtains 35.9% on ImageNet-1K at 10 IPC, whereas Table 1 quotes only 21.3% for SRe2L; full WMDD reaches 38.1% in that controlled ablation. This unexplained 14.6-point protocol or implementation gap means much of the apparent state-of-the-art margin cannot confidently be attributed to WMDD.

The factorial ablation reveals a large, unexplained interaction: Wasserstein matching with ordinary BN is substantially worse than CE+BN on Tiny ImageNet and ImageNet-1K, while PCBN reverses the result. Missing controls include k-means targets, uniform versus learned weights, PCBN added to faithfully reproduced strong baselines, alternative clustering methods, and sensitivity to barycenter initialization and iteration count.

The efficiency and reproducibility evidence remains incomplete. Timing is limited to ImageNette at 1 IPC and does not clearly account for the full 100-epoch teacher training, feature extraction, transport computation, FKD, and downstream training pipeline. The barycenter initialization, weight-update learning rate, exact use of learned weights during FKD, preprocessing, and several downstream settings are omitted or delegated to prior work. Cross-architecture results also lack uncertainty estimates.

The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-vppcmx2q/call-1d5d522a039642ef81eda85f4f523903/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation covers ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K at several IPC budgets. The reported ImageNet-1K results are strong: 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% at 10, 50, and 100 IPC, respectively, exceeding the best listed baselines.

The paper evaluates useful dimensions beyond same-architecture accuracy, including transfer to ResNet-50/101 and ViT models, runtime and memory, sliced Wasserstein distance, feature-layer choice, and regularization sensitivity.

Table 4 provides a factorial ablation of the feature objective and PCBN. The substantial PCBN improvements, particularly for the proposed feature objective, indicate that class-conditional activation statistics are practically valuable.

Code is linked, major optimization hyperparameters and hardware are reported, and repeated-run uncertainty is provided for the principal results. The supplement also acknowledges inherited dataset bias and potential efficiency benefits.
weaknesses: The central formulation is materially mischaracterized. For p=2, Equation 5 minimizes Wasserstein distance from one empirical distribution to an m-atomic distribution whose weights are free. Eliminating the column weights reduces the objective exactly to (1/n) sum_i min_j ||z_i-b_j||^2—ordinary feature-space k-means/vector quantization. Equation 11 is correspondingly a Lloyd-style centroid update. A barycenter of a single distribution is otherwise just that distribution. This substantially weakens the claimed optimal-transport originality.

No comparison is made against the mathematically equivalent k-means implementation, feature clustering with uniform or cluster-frequency weights, nearest-real exemplars, or other vector-quantization baselines. Nor are the learned weights ablated. Consequently, the experiments cannot establish that optimal transport machinery, rather than clustering targets, weighting, PCBN, or the inherited SRe2L/FKD pipeline, causes the gains.

The optimization derivation silently treats the optimal transport plan as fixed when declaring the objective quadratic and Equation 11 a Newton step. The full value function includes the dependence of the optimal plan on the support locations and is only piecewise smooth. The claimed convergence to a local optimum is unsupported, and division by w_j is undefined if simplex projection produces a zero weight.

The controlled evidence for the headline Wasserstein contribution is modest: with PCBN fixed, Table 4 improves over cross-entropy by only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 points on the three datasets. PCBN produces much larger gains for the proposed loss. Moreover, the CE+BN ablation reaches 35.9% on ImageNet-1K, far above the 21.3% reported for SRe2L despite ostensibly similar ingredients, leaving the source of the overall state-of-the-art improvement unclear.

Table 1 mostly mixes numbers reported by different papers with new WMDD runs; only one SRe2L setting is explicitly replicated. Training recipes, teacher checkpoints, augmentation/FKD variants, and uncertainty are therefore not demonstrated to be uniform. Cross-architecture results also lack error bars and do not clearly state whether every baseline was reevaluated using the same 20% synthetic validation protocol.

The supplementary theory gives separate standard bounds for W1 and MMD under unrelated assumptions but does not compare their constants or convergence rates. It is also disconnected from the implemented squared-W2 feature-space objective. The MMD discussion largely contrasts against linear-kernel mean matching, while the stripped empirical comparison in Figure 4 has no uncertainty and shows only small differences at 10 and 50 IPC.

The efficiency study does not clearly account end-to-end for teacher training on the full dataset, extraction and storage of all features and per-class BN statistics, barycenter computation, recovery, and FKD. Table 3 considers only ImageNette at 1 IPC and emphasizes image-update time, so the scalability claim is incompletely substantiated.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified in the manuscript, including initialization of B and the synthetic images, the weight-step size and schedule, projection and zero-weight handling, and exact downstream FKD/evaluation settings. Referring broadly to SRe2L does not make these choices self-contained. Overall, the strong empirical promise makes the decision close, but the unresolved equivalence to k-means and insufficient causal/fair-baseline evidence favor a borderline reject.

strengths: Strong large-scale results: WMDD substantially improves the reported 10–100 IPC accuracies on Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-1K, reaching 60.7% on ImageNet-1K at 100 IPC versus 57.9% for the strongest listed baseline.

The evaluation is broad for high-resolution dataset distillation, covering three datasets, four IPC budgets, cross-architecture transfer to ResNets and ViTs, runtime/memory, component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, and qualitative diversity.
The method is comparatively simple and practical. Per-class BatchNorm regularization is well motivated, and Table 4 provides evidence that it materially improves distilled-data quality.
The paper is clearly organized and provides repeated-run statistics for its principal results, implementation hyperparameters, a code URL, and a reasonable discussion of bias and energy implications.
weaknesses: The central mathematical novelty is questionable. With one input distribution, squared Euclidean cost, free support locations, and free target weights, Eq. 5 reduces to classwise k-means/optimal quantization: minimizing (1/n) sum_i min_j ||x_i-b_j||^2, with weights equal to cluster masses and Eq. 11 performing centroid updates. The paper neither acknowledges this equivalence nor compares against feature-space k-means, so it does not establish that a distinctly Wasserstein construction is responsible for the gains.

The metric comparison does not isolate the claimed contribution. Figure 4 compares different algorithmic frameworks rather than substituting metrics under a common pretrained encoder and regularizer. At 1 IPC, the proposed W2 center is simply the class mean and is therefore equivalent to linear-MMD mean matching under the same feature map, making the reported difference necessarily attributable to other pipeline choices. In Table 4, replacing CE with the Wasserstein-derived target adds only 0.8–1.7 points with PCBN, whereas PCBN often contributes much larger gains.

The theoretical appendix gives standard expected-loss bounds for W1 and MMD but the implemented method optimizes W2 squared. It neither compares the unknown constants nor proves one bound tighter, and thus does not explain the asserted superiority of the proposed metric.

The empirical comparison is not fully controlled: most Table 1 baselines are taken from prior reports, while teacher training, FKD/relabeling, and evaluation details may differ. Several supporting studies, including cross-architecture and metric comparisons, lack uncertainty estimates. The efficiency table is limited to ImageNette at 1 IPC and does not clearly account for full teacher training, feature extraction, PCBN collection, or downstream FKD, weakening the ImageNet-scale efficiency claim.

Important reproducibility details are absent from the manuscript, including barycenter initialization, the subgradient learning rate, OT solver settings, handling of zero weights in Eq. 11, synthetic-image initialization, and the precise use of learned weights during FKD and classifier training. Referring subsequent stages to another paper only partially resolves this. Overall, the results are promising, but the missing k-means baseline and confounded attribution leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The method is computationally practical and clearly presented: it combines class-wise feature prototypes with per-class BatchNorm regularization while avoiding costly bilevel optimization. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-k_2eh9zf/call-ac16976a22384e7996c0bfc97a5aac71/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Results are strong across ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K. For example, WMDD obtains 57.6% and 60.7% on ImageNet-1K at 50/100 IPC, versus the strongest listed baselines at 53.5% and 57.9%.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, including four compression budgets, cross-architecture transfer to larger ResNets and ViTs, component ablations, runtime and memory measurements, hyperparameter sensitivity, and qualitative diversity comparisons.

Algorithms, principal hyperparameters, hardware, repeated-run statistics for the main results, use of POT, and a public code link provide a useful reproducibility foundation. The paper also acknowledges inherited dataset bias and potential efficiency benefits.
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing is questionable. Equation 5 uses a single input distribution, freely optimized support locations and weights, and squared Euclidean transport cost; this is the classical m-point Wasserstein quantization problem, equivalent to weighted k-means-style clustering, rather than the nontrivial multi-distribution barycenter illustrated in Figure 2. A direct k-means or feature-clustering baseline is essential for establishing originality.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the Wasserstein metric. Figure 4 compares modified versions of two different algorithmic frameworks, while the most controlled ablation shows only 0.8–1.7 percentage-point gains from Wasserstein targets over cross-entropy when PCBN is fixed. PCBN produces substantially larger gains. Comparisons against k-means prototypes and MMD under the identical pretrained encoder, PCBN, augmentation, and FKD pipeline are missing.

Appendix B does not theoretically establish an advantage over MMD: it juxtaposes standard Wasserstein and RKHS bounds with different assumptions and incomparable constants. It also analyzes W1, whereas the implemented barycenter uses squared Euclidean cost corresponding to W2 squared.

Algorithm 2 omits consequential details such as support initialization and the weight-update learning rate. Simplex projection can produce zero weights, for which the stated position update divides by zero. Treating the transport plan as fixed also does not justify calling 2wjI the global classical Hessian of the nonsmooth optimized-transport objective.

Most baseline values are imported rather than rerun within one controlled pipeline, despite differences in pretrained models and training machinery. Efficiency is measured only on ImageNette at 1 IPC, and the accounting of teacher training, barycenter computation, recovery, and FKD is unclear. Cross-architecture and several sensitivity results lack uncertainty estimates.

All datasets are ImageNet-derived classification benchmarks and all distillation uses a ResNet-18 teacher, so the broader claims of adaptability and practical applicability are not yet demonstrated for other domains, teacher families, or vision tasks.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem with a comparatively simple feature-prototype recovery pipeline, and it is generally clear and well organized. Code is linked, standard datasets and borrowed components are attributed, and the assessment is based on the complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-20bdas31/call-181fee6ecc6d4051987d7bc0b969f3a3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The reported moderate- and high-budget results are strong. On ImageNet-1K, WMDD obtains 38.2/57.6/60.7% at 10/50/100 IPC, improving over the best tabulated baselines by 6.1/4.1/2.7 points; the Tiny-ImageNet improvements are also large.
Cross-architecture results are promising: synthetic data distilled with ResNet-18 transfers better than the listed alternatives to deeper ResNets and two ViTs.
The ablation across three datasets, five-run PCBN study, layer analysis, regularization sweep, and sliced-Wasserstein comparison provide useful diagnostic evidence.
The paper acknowledges inherited dataset bias, and the synthetic-image visualizations suggest improved intra-class variety over SRe2L.
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing is questionable. With one source distribution, unrestricted support weights, at most m atoms, and squared Euclidean transport cost, Eq. 5-6 is exactly feature-space vector quantization: optimizing the masses yields cluster proportions and Eq. 11/38 is the centroid update used by k-means. The paper presents this as Wasserstein-barycenter machinery without acknowledging the equivalence or comparing against k-means, k-medoids, or simple feature clustering. This substantially weakens both originality and causal attribution.

The ablation indicates that PCBN is essential, while replacing CE targets with the proposed Wasserstein-derived targets under PCBN adds only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 points on ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K. There is no ablation of clustering, learned masses, initialization, or alternative prototype-selection methods, so the evidence does not establish that optimal transport is the source of the large headline gains.

The optimization analysis is incomplete. The stated Hessian is valid only while treating the optimal transport plan as fixed; the minimized OT objective changes plans and can be nonsmooth. Consequently, describing the update as a Newton step and asserting convergence to a local optimum requires conditions or analysis not supplied.

The theoretical appendix presents two standard bounds under different assumptions but never proves that the Wasserstein bound is tighter. It analyzes W1, whereas the implemented objective uses squared Euclidean cost corresponding to W2 squared. Thus it does not support the claimed metric superiority.

The main comparison largely imports numbers from prior papers while asserting identical settings; only one SRe2L setting is explicitly reproduced. Teacher training, augmentation, relabeling, and evaluation details can materially affect large-scale distillation results. Relevant MMD work such as M3D is discussed but not included in the benchmark, and Figure 4 is a single-dataset, no-error-bar comparison after removing pipeline components rather than a tightly controlled metric substitution.

The efficiency evidence is not end-to-end: Table 3 covers only ImageNette at 1 IPC and does not break out teacher training, feature extraction, per-class BN collection, barycenter computation, or FKD. This is insufficient to substantiate broad computational-efficiency claims on ImageNet-1K.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the code link: barycenter initialization, the weight-step learning rate eta, simplex projection and solver settings, random seeds, precise downstream training schedule, and use of learned masses are not fully specified. Cross-architecture and sliced-Wasserstein results also lack uncertainty estimates.

The t-SNE plots and selected visual examples do not quantitatively establish diversity or reduced overfitting. Overall, the empirical results are promising enough to make the decision close, but the unrecognized k-means equivalence and missing controls leave a slight preference for rejection.

Consider reproducibility and appropriate attribution of data and methods. Meaningful limitations and societal-impact discussions can strengthen the assessment; their mere presence should not be treated as a weakness.

Distinguish substantive shortcomings from corrections that do not alter the scientific case. Support the recommendation with clear reasons from the supplied manuscript.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Reject
Consequential shortcomings prevent a convincing case for acceptance.

3 = Borderline Reject

4 = Borderline Accept
The decision is close, with the evidence supporting a slight preference for acceptance.

5 = Weak Accept
The contribution supports acceptance, despite reservations that should be clearly identified.

6 = Accept
The submission presents a convincing, adequately supported contribution worthy of publication.

strengths: The paper addresses the important problem of scalable dataset distillation and proposes a comparatively simple pipeline combining class-conditional feature prototypes with per-class BatchNorm (PCBN) regularization.
The reported results are strong against the selected baselines, including 60.7% ImageNet-1K accuracy at 100 IPC and improvements across the tested ResNet and ViT evaluation architectures.
The empirical study covers three dataset scales and several IPC budgets, with component ablations, sensitivity analyses, runtime measurements, and useful qualitative examples.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, cites the datasets and major antecedents, provides a code link and some implementation details, and acknowledges bias and environmental considerations. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-0guthtag/call-b0d01e82b2824d62aa7ba2583796c750/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central formulation is substantially mischaracterized. Equation 5 uses one input distribution and freely optimizes the support locations and weights under squared Euclidean transport cost. Eliminating the free weights yields the standard quantization objective (per-class k-means in teacher-feature space), not the multi-distribution Wasserstein barycenter illustrated in Figure 2. The essential k-means/Lloyd baseline is absent, severely weakening both originality and attribution.

The image-recovery objective in Equation 15 does not directly match real and synthetic distributions with a Wasserstein loss; it matches individual synthetic features to precomputed centroids and adds PCBN. Table 4 suggests PCBN is the dominant improvement—for ImageNet-1K it raises the Wasserstein configuration from 26.8% to 38.1%, whereas replacing CE with the proposed target under PCBN raises 36.4% only to 38.1%. PCBN is not evaluated when added to the strongest competing pipelines.

The MMD comparison is confounded. At 1 IPC, the proposed squared-Wasserstein quantizer is exactly the class feature mean, also the target induced by linear-kernel MMD, yet Figure 4 reports a large difference between separately engineered pipelines. This cannot support the claimed superiority of the metric.

The theoretical appendix analyzes W1, while the implemented derivation and cost matrix use squared Euclidean W2. Its generic Wasserstein and MMD bounds rely on unverified Lipschitz/RKHS assumptions, do not estimate their constants, and imply no ordering between the metrics; consequently, they do not explain the empirical claims.

The optimization argument is incomplete. Equations 11 and 35 treat the optimal transport plan as fixed when forming a Hessian, although the minimized OT value changes plans and is only piecewise smooth. Conditions for the claimed Newton step and local convergence are not supplied, and zero learned weights would make the update undefined.

Most competing numbers are copied from prior papers, despite the claim of identical settings. Differences in teachers, preprocessing, augmentation, FKD/relabeling, training schedules, and uncertainty are not reconciled. The cross-architecture study also lacks repeated-run errors and does not clearly explain how its 20% synthetic holdout protocol was applied to every baseline.

The scalability evidence is incomplete: the detailed resource comparison is only for ImageNette at 1 IPC and does not itemize teacher training, full feature extraction, OT computation, FKD label generation/storage, and downstream training. End-to-end ImageNet-1K cost is therefore not established.

Reproduction of the central stage requires details absent from the manuscript, including barycenter initialization, the weight learning rate, projection and OT-solver settings, zero-weight handling, and the precise use of learned weights during FKD. The code link helps, but the paper is not sufficiently self-contained.

The t-SNE and image grids are suggestive but do not establish distribution coverage or diversity. No quantitative diversity, nearest-neighbor memorization, or leakage analysis supports the stronger claims about representing the real distribution or mitigating privacy concerns.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical problem and reports strong results across ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K, including substantial gains at several 10–100 IPC settings.
The combination of pretrained feature targets, learned prototype weights, and per-class BatchNorm statistics is simple, scalable, and produces visually plausible synthetic images.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, covering multiple budgets, cross-architecture transfer, runtime and memory, component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, sliced Wasserstein distance, and repeated runs for the main results.

The manuscript is generally clear, supplies equations, algorithms, implementation hyperparameters, and a public code link, and acknowledges bias in the source data. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2ks26noz/call-058e427171344ebfbe249dc8e4bf73f7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central novelty is questionable. Equation 5 is not a Wasserstein barycenter under Definition 2: it is a one-distribution, support-constrained Wasserstein approximation. With free weights and squared Euclidean cost, it reduces to standard vector quantization/k-means in teacher feature space. This equivalence is neither acknowledged nor evaluated against k-means, prototype-selection, or feature-space coreset baselines. Figure 2 concerns barycenters of multiple distributions and therefore does not justify the actual N=1 construction.

The evidence does not isolate a benefit from the Wasserstein metric. With PCBN fixed, Table 4 shows only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 point improvements over cross-entropy, while Wasserstein with ordinary BN is worse than cross-entropy on two datasets. The much larger PCBN interaction suggests that teacher inversion and regularization may drive the headline gains.

The MMD comparison is not controlled: Figure 4 changes or removes augmentation and FKD components and contrasts against a separate DM implementation. It primarily attacks linear mean matching rather than comparing the same pipeline using a characteristic kernel, scalable MMD estimator, or simple k-means objective. Consequently, it cannot support the broad metric-superiority narrative.

The theoretical appendix gives generic but incomparable bounds. It analyzes W1 while the method optimizes squared W2, assumes an unsubstantiated Lipschitz labeling/loss function, and never compares the unknown Lipschitz and RKHS constants. It establishes no dominance over MMD; the quadratic-cost argument also overlooks common linear-time or minibatch MMD estimators.

The optimization derivation treats the optimal transport plan as fixed when declaring the objective quadratic and its Hessian equal to 2wjI. Since the plan changes with prototype positions, this is only a conditional, piecewise result; the objective can be nonsmooth. The claimed local convergence is unsupported, and zero-weight prototypes are not handled despite division by wj.

Experimental comparability and reproducibility remain uncertain. Table 1 mostly imports reported baseline numbers and explicitly reproduces only SRe2L on ImageNette, without demonstrating matched teacher, augmentation, relabeling, or evaluation recipes. Cross-architecture results have no uncertainty estimates. Prototype initialization, barycenter learning rate and projection details, and the exact use of learned weights during FKD are also unspecified. These omissions are consequential because the reported advantage may depend strongly on the surrounding recipe.

Please review the following manuscript. I've poured years of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem with a conceptually simple pipeline combining class-conditional feature representatives, synthetic-image recovery, and per-class BatchNorm (PCBN) regularization.

The empirical results are strong: WMDD reports 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% on ImageNet-1K at 10, 50, and 100 IPC, respectively, with small variation over three runs and substantial improvements over the listed scalable baselines.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, covering three high-resolution datasets, four IPC budgets, transfer from ResNet-18 to deeper ResNets and ViTs, a two-by-two component ablation, alternative metrics, sensitivity analysis, runtime, and qualitative diversity.

PCBN is intuitive and appears genuinely effective. In Table 4, adding PCBN to the cross-entropy formulation improves all three datasets, while the full PCBN-plus-Wasserstein configuration performs best.

The presentation is readable, and the supplement provides equations, algorithms, hyperparameters, a code link, extensive visualizations, appropriate dataset/software citations, and a sensible discussion of inherited bias and potential efficiency benefits. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-swgv5f_r/call-8dd2a0ca2c6349e08b84009a05558437/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing substantially overstates the novelty. Equation 5 is a support-constrained approximation of one distribution (N=1), not a nontrivial Wasserstein barycenter. Moreover, with squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized atom weights, eliminating the weights and transport plan reduces the objective to standard k-means/vector quantization in feature space. The absence of a k-means or comparable prototype baseline is therefore consequential.

The theoretical appendix analyzes W1, whereas the implemented cost and updates correspond to squared W2. Its generic Lipschitz and RKHS bounds do not compare the unknown constants or prove a Wasserstein advantage, and Figure 2 concerns barycenters of multiple distributions unlike the actual N=1 method.

Algorithm 2 is underspecified and potentially inconsistent: it updates the weights after computing a transport plan and then appears to reuse that plan for the position update, although its column marginals correspond to the old weights. Initialization, the barycenter learning rate and schedule, zero-weight handling, and conditions behind the asserted convergence/Newton update are also missing.

The ablation weakens attribution to the headline contribution. With PCBN fixed, Wasserstein improves over cross-entropy by only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 points across the three datasets, while it is markedly worse than cross-entropy with ordinary BN on Tiny ImageNet and ImageNet-1K. The much larger gains come from PCBN, and there are no controls for ordinary k-means, uniform versus learned weights, class means, or other clustering objectives.

The MMD comparison is not controlled tightly enough: the reported figure compares stripped-down versions of different frameworks, while the claimed near-random result from directly substituting MMD is not reported in detail. Thus it does not isolate the metric from kernels, encoders, augmentations, PCBN, and FKD.

Table 1 mainly combines numbers reported by other papers, contains many missing cells, and does not establish that teacher training, augmentation, relabeling, or evaluation schedules are identical. Cross-architecture results lack uncertainty, and the unusual 20% synthetic-data validation protocol is not described sufficiently for verifying equal treatment of baselines.

The efficiency table evidently omits the full-data teacher training, feature extraction, and per-class-statistics costs, making comparisons against methods that do not require a pretrained teacher incomplete. Important recovery and FKD details are delegated to prior work, and all distillation experiments use a BatchNorm-based ResNet-18 teacher, limiting support for broader adaptability claims.

The claimed Hessian 2w_j I and Newton step treat the optimal transport plan as fixed; the minimized OT objective is only piecewise quadratic because the plan changes with the support. Initialization, the weight step size, empty/near-zero-weight handling, and convergence sensitivity are not reported.","The supplementary theory does not support the claimed metric advantage. It analyzes W_1 while the implemented objective uses squared Euclidean transport/W_2^2, and merely presents standard Wasserstein and MMD bounds under different, unquantified assumptions. The crucial k-means baseline, uniform-versus-learned-weight ablation, and controlled replacement with characteristic-kernel MMD are absent. strengths: The method delivers strong high-resolution results. On ImageNet-1K, WMDD reaches 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% at 10, 50, and 100 IPC, respectively, outperforming the listed baselines, with similarly strong medium/high-IPC results on Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNette.

The evaluation covers three datasets, four compression budgets, cross-architecture transfer to deeper ResNets and ViTs, runtime/memory, component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, feature layers, and qualitative diversity. Most primary results include repeated-run uncertainty.

Per-class BatchNorm regularization is intuitive and empirically effective. The synthetic images are recognizable and visibly more varied than SRe2L examples, while the cross-architecture results suggest practical utility beyond the distillation backbone.

The paper is generally clear, provides algorithms and major recovery hyperparameters, attributes the main borrowed components, links code, and includes a reasonable discussion of bias and environmental impact.
weaknesses: The central mathematical construction is substantially mischaracterized. With squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized synthetic weights, Eq. 5 reduces exactly to feature-space vector quantization: min_{B,w} W_2^2(P,Q) = (1/n) sum_i min_j ||z_i-b_j||^2, i.e., k-means, with weights equal to cluster proportions. It is not meaningfully a multi-distribution Wasserstein barycenter. The paper neither acknowledges this equivalence nor compares against ordinary k-means/Lloyd updates, making the claimed optimal-transport originality and source of the gains unclear.

The optimization analysis is incomplete. The claimed Hessian 2w_j I and Newton step treat the optimal transport plan as fixed; the minimized OT objective is only piecewise quadratic because the plan changes with the support. Thus the stated convergence to a local optimum is not established. Moreover, free weights can be obtained directly from cluster assignments, making the projected subgradient procedure appear unnecessary. Initialization, the weight step size, empty/near-zero-weight handling, and convergence sensitivity are not reported.

The supplementary theory does not support the claimed metric advantage. It analyzes W_1 while the implemented objective uses squared Euclidean transport/W_2^2, and merely presents standard Wasserstein and MMD bounds under different, unquantified assumptions. It neither shows that the Wasserstein bound is tighter nor connects rigorously to training on inverted feature prototypes.

Experimental attribution is insufficient for the main claim. Table 4 shows that PCBN supplies most of the improvement, while Wasserstein matching adds only 0.8-1.7 points over CE when PCBN is fixed. The crucial k-means baseline, uniform-versus-learned-weight ablation, and controlled replacement with characteristic-kernel MMD are absent. Figure 4 instead compares different vanilla pipelines on only Tiny-ImageNet, without uncertainty; this is not a clean metric comparison.

The main comparison mixes reported results from different papers while asserting identical settings, and several entries lack uncertainties. End-to-end cost including teacher training, feature extraction, OT computation, and FKD/relabeling is not isolated. Evaluation/FKD details are largely deferred to SRe2L, the use and storage cost of learned weights/soft labels is unclear, and the cross-architecture experiment has no error bars and ambiguously holds out 20% of the fixed synthetic-data budget. These gaps limit reproducibility and confidence in the scalability and fairness claims.

strengths: The practical pipeline—classwise compact feature targets combined with weighted per-class BatchNorm regularization—is simple, scalable, and intuitively promotes intra-class coverage.

The evaluation is broad for large-scale dataset distillation, covering ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K at four IPC budgets. WMDD obtains strong results in most nontrivial settings, including 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% on ImageNet-1K at 10, 50, and 100 IPC.

The manuscript provides cross-architecture evaluation, component ablations, hyperparameter and feature-layer studies, a sliced-Wasserstein comparison, runtime and memory measurements, and useful qualitative visualizations. Main and ablation results include repeated-run uncertainty.
The presentation is generally clear, relevant datasets and methods are cited, implementation hyperparameters are partially documented, and a code repository is provided.
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing substantially obscures a simpler interpretation: with one target distribution, free support and weights, and squared Euclidean transport cost, Eq. 5 is optimal vector quantization and reduces to classwise k-means. The paper neither discusses or attributes this equivalence nor includes a k-means baseline, materially weakening its originality and the claim that Wasserstein geometry is responsible for the gains.

The optimization analysis is imprecise. Because the optimal transport plan changes with the support positions, the value function is only piecewise quadratic and can be nondifferentiable; therefore the claimed classical Hessian and Newton interpretation are not globally valid. The asserted convergence to a local optimum is unsupported, and the update is undefined if projected optimization produces a zero weight.

The Wasserstein-versus-MMD evidence is not controlled. Figure 4 compares different algorithmic frameworks after removing selected components rather than changing only the metric. The appendix presents standard W1 and RKHS bounds with incomparable constants and assumptions, while the implemented objective uses squared W2; it consequently does not establish superiority of the actual method over MMD.

Attribution of the empirical gains remains incomplete. With PCBN fixed, replacing CE by the Wasserstein feature target improves accuracy by only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 points on the three datasets. There are no comparisons against feature-space k-means, equal versus learned weights, or PCBN inserted into the strongest existing pipeline, making it difficult to separate the effects of Wasserstein quantization, PCBN, the pretrained teacher, and FKD.

Important reproducibility and efficiency details are missing, including barycenter-support initialization, the projected-subgradient step size and schedule, zero-weight handling, and the exact use of learned weights during FKD and downstream training. Most baseline numbers are imported, cross-architecture results lack uncertainty, and no complete end-to-end ImageNet-1K cost accounting is given for teacher pretraining, feature extraction, recovery, and relabeling.

The reported results are strong: at 100 IPC, WMDD reaches 87.1%, 61.0%, and 60.7% on ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K, respectively, approaching the corresponding full-data teacher accuracies.

The evaluation spans three high-resolution datasets, four image budgets, ResNet and ViT transfer, efficiency measurements, alternative metrics, feature layers, regularization strengths, and component ablations.
Cross-architecture results are encouraging: synthetic data distilled with ResNet-18 performs best among the compared methods on all five evaluation architectures in Table 2.

The presentation is generally clear, and reproducibility is aided by algorithms, hardware and hyperparameter information, repeated trials, use of a standard optimal-transport library, and an available code repository. The societal-impact discussion appropriately acknowledges inherited dataset bias.
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing is questionable: Eq. 5 uses a single input distribution, so the support-constrained objective is more accurately Wasserstein vector quantization than a conventional barycenter. With freely optimized target weights and squared Euclidean cost, it reduces to a class-wise k-means-style problem, and the position update is essentially a Lloyd centroid update. The absence of a direct feature-space k-means/quantization baseline leaves the transport-specific novelty unclear.

The theoretical appendix analyzes W1, whereas the implemented cost is squared Euclidean and therefore corresponds to W2 squared. Its W1 and MMD bounds contain unrelated, unknown constants under strong Lipschitz/RKHS assumptions, so they do not establish that the implemented Wasserstein objective should outperform MMD.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently controlled. Table 1 mostly imports reported results rather than rerunning methods in one pipeline. More concerningly, the CE+BN ablation obtains 35.9% on ImageNet-1K at 10 IPC, while the conceptually corresponding listed SRe2L baseline is only 21.3%; this large unexplained discrepancy weakens the headline comparison.

When PCBN is fixed, replacing CE with the Wasserstein target improves 10-IPC accuracy by only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 points across the three datasets. Meanwhile, the MMD experiment removes components native to the MMD baseline and reports no uncertainty, so it does not cleanly isolate metric choice. Controlled comparisons with k-means and characteristic-kernel MMD under the identical recovery and evaluation pipeline are needed.

The efficiency evidence is limited to ImageNette at 1 IPC and Tiny-ImageNet for the sliced-Wasserstein comparison. End-to-end ImageNet-1K time and memory, clearly including teacher training, feature extraction, PCBN collection, transport computation, recovery, and relabeling, are not reported.

Several details needed for independent reproduction are missing or delegated to prior work, including barycenter initialization, the projected-subgradient learning rate and schedule, feature normalization, precise OT solver settings, and how learned weights are used in the CE ablation and FKD stage. The code link only partially mitigates this.

Cross-architecture evaluation covers only one IPC setting, lacks uncertainty estimates, and uses a 20% synthetic validation holdout without fully specifying whether every baseline was reevaluated identically. Dependence on the full-data pretrained teacher, weaker 1-IPC results on two datasets, and relatively poor ViT transfer also deserve fuller discussion.

Table 1 reports strong results across ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K, leading 10 of the 12 displayed IPC settings and showing particularly substantial gains at moderate and large budgets.

The evaluation is broader than a single benchmark: it includes ResNet-to-ResNet/ViT transfer, component ablations, runtime and memory measurements, sliced-Wasserstein comparisons, hyperparameter sensitivity, and extensive visualizations.

weaknesses: The central formulation is overstated. Equation 5 uses a single input distribution, so the constrained problem is an m-point Wasserstein projection or optimal quantization problem—essentially k-means-like under squared Euclidean cost—rather than the usual barycenter of multiple distributions. A comparison with class-wise k-means, medoids, or other feature prototypes is essential for establishing novelty and benefit.

The experiments do not cleanly attribute the gains to Wasserstein geometry. In Table 4, replacing CE with the Wasserstein target under PCBN improves accuracy by only 0.8–1.7 points, while interactions with PCBN are much larger in some settings. Moreover, CE+BN obtains 35.9% on ImageNet-1K at 10 IPC, far above the 21.3% SRe2L result in Table 1, without explaining which remaining pipeline changes cause this gap. Uniform-weight and no-barycenter ablations are also absent.

The theoretical appendix does not support the headline comparison: it analyzes W1 while the algorithm uses squared W2, gives standard bounds containing incomparable unknown constants, and does not connect teacher-feature quantization and image inversion to the risk of a model trained from scratch. It therefore cannot establish superiority over MMD.

The optimization justification is incomplete. The stated Hessian treats the optimal transport plan as fixed even though it changes with the support positions, so the update is a surrogate/Lloyd-type step rather than a justified Newton step for the true nonsmooth value function. Joint convergence is asserted without proof, and zero learned weights would make the update singular.

The MMD experiment is not an apples-to-apples metric substitution: it compares altered 'vanilla' frameworks and mainly targets linear-kernel mean matching. Table 1 otherwise combines mostly reported baseline numbers without adequately documenting equivalence of training, augmentation, relabeling, resolution, and evaluation protocols. Cross-architecture results have no uncertainty estimates, and the use of a 20% synthetic validation split is not clearly matched for all baselines.

strengths: The method is clearly presented and practically motivated: classwise teacher features are summarized into multiple targets, inverted into synthetic images, and regularized using per-class BatchNorm statistics. The algorithms and diagrams make the pipeline easy to follow. This assessment is based on the supplied manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2sa3cmrc/call-b001f287a2ce4f6b8ac00ee82b4a31c7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The reported results are strong and broad: experiments cover ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K at four compression budgets, with particularly large gains at 10–100 IPC. The ImageNet-1K results of 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% at 10, 50, and 100 IPC are practically significant if the comparison is controlled.
Cross-architecture evaluation spans three ResNets and two ViTs, supporting the claim that the distilled data are not useful only for the distillation architecture.

The paper includes factorial ablations, sensitivity analyses, an alternative sliced-Wasserstein experiment, runtime measurements, repeated runs for the main results, extensive visualizations, implementation hyperparameters, a code link, and a reasonable discussion of source-data bias.
weaknesses: The central novelty is substantially overstated. Equation 5 is not a Wasserstein barycenter problem in the usual sense: it has one input distribution and constrains the output to m atoms. With freely optimized output weights and squared Euclidean cost, minimizing over the transport plan and weights reduces exactly to classwise k-means/optimal quantization: each real feature is assigned to its nearest support and each support becomes a cluster centroid. No k-means, Lloyd, or feature-clustering baseline is provided, and the relevant quantization interpretation is neither discussed nor appropriately attributed.

The optimization derivation is not technically sound as written. With weights fixed, the optimal transport plan changes with the support positions, so the minimized OT objective is not globally quadratic and its Hessian is not simply 2w_j I. That expression holds only while treating the transport plan as fixed. Consequently, the claimed Newton step and convergence to a local optimum are not justified; zero learned weights would also make the update undefined.

The evidence that the Wasserstein metric itself causes the gains is inadequate. Table 4 compares the proposed target-matching loss with cross-entropy, not with a controlled MMD or k-means counterpart. Figure 4 compares different algorithmic frameworks, while the claimed near-random result from directly replacing Wasserstein with MMD is not reported with sufficient settings or statistics. PCBN appears to be the dominant factor, whereas Wasserstein adds only 0.8–1.7 points over CE when PCBN is fixed.

The theoretical appendix does not establish superiority: it states standard, separate bounds involving unknown and incomparable constants, analyzes W1 while the implemented objective uses squared Euclidean W2, and does not connect the bound to training a model on the resulting synthetic set. Its claim that characteristic-kernel MMD is necessarily quadratic also overlooks scalable estimators and approximations.

The state-of-the-art comparison is not fully controlled. Most baseline numbers are copied from prior papers despite the assertion of identical settings, and evaluation recipes, relabeling/FKD procedures, and uncertainty reporting may differ. The manuscript lacks the most important simple control implied by its formulation: applying classwise k-means to teacher features and using the same inversion, PCBN, and downstream training pipeline.

The scalability evidence is weaker than the claims. The principal timing comparison uses ImageNette at 1 IPC, where the proposed one-point quantizer is merely the class mean and transport is trivial. Costs for training the full-data teacher, extracting features, computing barycenters, recovery, and FKD are not clearly separated, and no end-to-end ImageNet-1K time or memory result is given.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified despite the code link, including barycenter-support initialization, the projected-subgradient learning rate and projection, handling of zero weights, exact PCBN-statistic collection, and how learned weights affect FKD and final training. The t-SNE and image-diversity evidence is qualitative and lacks a quantitative coverage or nearest-neighbor/memorization analysis. Overall, the strong empirical results make the decision close, but the missing k-means-equivalence analysis and controlled baselines prevent a convincing scientific case for the claimed Wasserstein contribution.

The SOTA table largely mixes numbers reported by other papers rather than controlled reruns with the same teacher, augmentation, FKD, and evaluation protocol. Cross-architecture and sliced-Wasserstein tables also lack uncertainty estimates, and the 20% synthetic validation protocol is insufficiently specified.

The efficiency evidence does not clearly include teacher pretraining, extraction of all real features and per-class BN statistics, barycenter construction, or FKD/relabeling costs and storage.
