strengths: WMDD is simple, intuitive, and scalable: it combines class-wise feature-space optimal transport targets with per-class BatchNorm regularization in a practical synthesis pipeline.
The reported results are strong, particularly on ImageNet-1K, where WMDD reaches 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% at 10/50/100 IPC and consistently improves over the listed scalable baselines.

The evaluation is broad in useful dimensions, including three high-resolution datasets, ResNet-to-ResNet/ViT transfer, runtime and memory, component ablations, sliced-Wasserstein comparison, layer and regularization sensitivity, and informative synthetic-image visualizations.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, cites its datasets and major dependencies, provides implementation hyperparameters and a code URL, and includes a reasonable discussion of bias and environmental impact. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-h11esnyc/call-4fb4a3c29303436ba5be8a1d7674eb4e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central construction is mischaracterized as a Wasserstein barycenter. Equation 5 has only one input distribution; restricting its output to m freely weighted atoms makes it Wasserstein quantization. Under the stated squared-Euclidean cost, optimizing free supports and weights is equivalent to k-means/vector quantization. The paper neither acknowledges this equivalence nor compares against class-wise k-means feature targets, leaving the main originality claim unsubstantiated.

The optimization analysis is not technically convincing. The claimed Hessian 2w_jI treats the optimal transport plan as fixed, although that plan changes with the support positions; consequently, the centroid update is not generally a Newton step for the stated value function. Convergence claims lack conditions, and zero learned weights would make Equation 11 undefined.

The supplementary theory analyzes W1 while WMDD actually uses squared W2 costs. Its standard Wasserstein and RKHS generalization bounds contain incomparable, uncontrolled constants and therefore do not establish superiority over MMD. The claim that expressive-kernel MMD necessarily requires quadratic full-dataset computation also overlooks minibatching, linear-time estimators, and random-feature approximations.

The ablation indicates that PCBN, rather than the Wasserstein component, supplies most of the improvement: with PCBN, replacing cross-entropy by Wasserstein improves accuracy by only 0.8–1.7 points, whereas PCBN itself often changes accuracy by much more. Strong baselines using the same pretrained teacher, PCBN, feature inversion, FKD, and ordinary k-means or other clustering targets are essential.

Experimental fairness and efficiency accounting are insufficiently established. Table 1 primarily combines reported baseline results rather than rerunning methods in one controlled pipeline. Table 3 does not clearly include teacher training, full-data feature extraction, barycenter computation, and FKD/relabeling, even though teacher training is part of Algorithm 1 and competing DC/DM methods do not require that same squeeze stage.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including barycenter initialization, the weight-update learning rate and projection procedure, handling of empty supports, and precisely how learned weights enter FKD and downstream training. Cross-architecture and sliced-Wasserstein results also lack uncertainty estimates, and cross-architecture testing is limited to one dataset and IPC setting. Overall, the empirical promise is substantial, but these concerns slightly outweigh the case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses the important practical problem of scalable dataset distillation with a simple pipeline combining class-wise feature representatives, image inversion, and per-class BatchNorm regularization.

The reported absolute results are strong, especially at moderate and high IPC: WMDD reaches 60.7% on ImageNet-1K at 100 IPC and generally improves over the listed large-scale baselines. Cross-architecture results also show consistent transfer gains.

The experiments cover three high-resolution datasets, several IPC budgets, repeated trials for the main results, efficiency, component ablations, layer and regularization sensitivity, sliced Wasserstein, and useful qualitative visualizations.

The presentation is generally clear, with algorithms and additional implementation details in the supplement. Public code, appropriate dataset/method citations, and a relevant discussion of inherited bias support reproducibility and responsible use.
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing is questionable. Equation 5 uses a one-input Wasserstein “barycenter” with an m-point support constraint. With squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized weights, this reduces to standard optimal quantization/k-means: each real feature is assigned to a nearest center, the weights are cluster proportions, and the position update computes cluster centroids. The paper neither acknowledges this equivalence nor compares against a basic feature-space k-means/prototype baseline, substantially weakening its originality and Wasserstein-specific claims.

The headline baseline comparison does not cleanly isolate the proposed contribution. At ImageNet-1K/10 IPC, the paper's own CE+standard-BN ablation obtains 35.9%, whereas Table 1 quotes only 21.3% for SRe2L, even though CE+BN is presented as the prior recipe. Only the ImageNette SRe2L result was rerun. Changes to recovery hyperparameters, weight decay, weighting, or FKD may therefore explain much of the reported 38.2% result; strong baselines need evaluation within the same pipeline.

The optimization analysis overstates its guarantees. After minimizing over the transport plan, the objective is not globally quadratic in each support position because the optimal plan changes with the positions; consequently, the stated Hessian, “Newton step,” and convergence to a local optimum require qualifications or proof.

The supplementary theory analyzes W1 while the implemented objective uses squared W2 cost. Its generic Wasserstein and MMD bounds contain incomparable unknown constants and unverified assumptions, so they establish no superiority. The statement that W1 captures discrepancies in all moments is also too strong.

The metric ablation is not decisive: once PCBN is used, Wasserstein improves over CE by only 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 points at 10 IPC. The MMD experiment changes pipelines and primarily targets linear-kernel mean matching rather than providing a controlled comparison to a characteristic or scalable MMD estimator.

Efficiency and reproducibility remain incomplete. The runtime accounting does not clearly include teacher training, full feature extraction, OT computation, and FKD/relabeling, while barycenter initialization, subgradient learning rate, projection details, and the precise use of learned weights during student training are unspecified. Moreover, all three datasets are ImageNet-derived, limiting evidence for broader distributional generalization.

strengths: The work addresses an important problem—scalable dataset distillation—and presents a simple feature-space prototype matching and per-class BatchNorm pipeline. The manuscript is generally readable and well organized. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-o058tnsx/call-cdf9c01a67c74af0b44c7919d3d82e09/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Reported results are strong: WMDD reaches 41.8/59.4/61.0% on Tiny ImageNet and 38.2/57.6/60.7% on ImageNet-1K at 10/50/100 IPC, respectively, outperforming the listed baselines in most settings.

The paper includes cross-architecture evaluation, component ablations, regularization and feature-layer sensitivity studies, a sliced-Wasserstein comparison, efficiency measurements, and synthetic-image visualizations.
Algorithms, major recovery hyperparameters, a code link, and a reasonable discussion of bias and environmental impact are provided.
weaknesses: The central formulation is insufficiently distinguished from ordinary feature-space k-means. With freely optimized synthetic weights, eliminating the weights and transport plan from Eqs. 5–8 yields the quantization objective averaging each real feature's squared distance to its nearest prototype. The one-distribution construction is also not a conventional Wasserstein barycenter. This equivalence is neither acknowledged nor compared against a k-means-centroid baseline using the identical inversion and PCBN pipeline, substantially weakening the originality claim and attribution of gains to optimal transport.

The claimed Newton derivation treats the optimal transport plan as constant when differentiating. The reduced OT objective is generally nonsmooth and only piecewise quadratic because the optimal plan changes with prototype positions; consequently, the stated Hessian and convergence-to-a-local-optimum claims require qualification or proof.

The theoretical appendix establishes a standard bound for a fixed hypothesis using W1, whereas the implemented method uses squared Euclidean transport corresponding to W2-squared in learned feature space. It does not analyze training on the distilled set or demonstrate superiority over MMD; its assumptions and constants are not verified. The KL/MMD/Wasserstein visualization is also missing kernel, smoothing, optimization, and support details.

The metric comparison is confounded by different algorithmic pipelines. At one IPC, a single W2 prototype is simply the class feature mean, which is also the target of linear-kernel MMD, so the large reported difference cannot by itself be attributed to the metric. Moreover, Table 4 shows that replacing CE with the Wasserstein target adds only 0.8–1.7 points with PCBN, while PCBN supplies much larger gains; no k-means, uniform-weight, or matched characteristic-kernel control is given.

Most baseline numbers in Table 1 are imported from prior work. The paper does not establish that teacher training, augmentation, relabeling/FKD, evaluation schedules, and model selection are identical. Cross-architecture and several sensitivity results lack uncertainty estimates, further limiting the strength of comparative conclusions.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: barycenter initialization, weight-step learning rate and schedule, projection and OT-solver details, random seeds, exact use of learned weights during FKD, and complete recovery/evaluation settings are not specified. Referring broadly to SRe2L does not resolve these ambiguities.

The efficiency study covers only ImageNette at one IPC, and it is unclear whether total time fully includes teacher training, feature extraction, and barycenter construction. The t-SNE and selected visual examples provide weak evidence for diversity, with no quantitative diversity or nearest-neighbor/memorization analysis. Overall, the empirical numbers are promising, but the missing decisive controls and conceptual issues slightly favor rejection.

strengths: The method is simple and practically relevant: class-wise feature summarization, synthetic-image inversion, and per-class BatchNorm regularization form a scalable pipeline for high-resolution dataset distillation.

The empirical results are strong, particularly at 10–100 IPC: WMDD improves substantially over the listed scalable baselines on Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-1K and approaches the reported full-data teacher accuracies at 100 IPC.

The evaluation includes multiple datasets and budgets, three-run uncertainty estimates, cross-architecture transfer to ResNets and ViTs, and useful ablations over PCBN, feature layers, regularization strength, and sliced Wasserstein distance.

The manuscript is generally clear, provides algorithms and core hyperparameters, cites the datasets and inherited SRe2L/FKD components, releases code, and acknowledges bias and environmental implications.
weaknesses: The central formulation is overstated as a Wasserstein barycenter contribution. Equation 5 uses only one input distribution with a support-size constraint; for the squared Euclidean cost and freely learned weights, this is optimal quantization and is essentially class-wise k-means in feature space. No k-means, nearest-centroid, or representative-sample baseline is provided, making the claimed originality difficult to establish.

After the target supports are computed, Equation 12 is ordinary pointwise squared feature matching rather than a Wasserstein objective. Table 4 shows only modest gains over cross-entropy when both use PCBN, while the large gain arises from their interaction. The paper therefore does not convincingly isolate whether optimal transport, feature clustering, PCBN, or the inherited SRe2L/FKD pipeline causes the reported improvements.

The theoretical appendix analyzes a standard W1 loss bound, whereas the implemented method uses squared Euclidean transport corresponding to W2 squared. Its comparison with MMD relies on different assumptions and incomparable constants, so it cannot establish superiority. The position-update derivation also treats the optimal transport plan as fixed when stating the Hessian and does not justify the claimed convergence as the plan changes.

The baseline evidence is not sufficiently controlled. Table 1 mixes externally reported results with a single replication while asserting identical settings, and teacher training, augmentations, relabeling, and evaluation protocols can materially affect large-scale distillation. The MMD comparison removes unspecified engineering components and does not demonstrate matched encoders or optimization budgets, so it is not a clean metric-level comparison.

The efficiency claim is incompletely supported: Table 3 covers only ImageNette at 1 IPC and appears not to include the 100-epoch teacher-training cost, while the proposed pipeline additionally requires full-data feature extraction, exact transport solves, and FKD. End-to-end time and memory on ImageNet-1K, where scalability matters most, are absent.

Important reproducibility details are omitted from the manuscript, including barycenter-support initialization, the projected-subgradient learning rate and schedule, projection and OT-solver settings, handling of near-zero weights, and precisely how learned weights enter FKD and downstream training. Robustness to teacher architecture, teacher quality, and initialization is also untested.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-bc8mw2xx/call-00699bdee8514e3aa5ebb2ea4ef5e552/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem with a conceptually simple pipeline that scales to high-resolution datasets.

The reported results are strong. On ImageNet-1K, WMDD obtains 38.2, 57.6, and 60.7% at 10, 50, and 100 IPC, improving over the best tabulated baselines; the gains on Tiny-ImageNet are particularly large. Results are reported across three datasets and several compression budgets.

The evaluation includes useful breadth: cross-architecture transfer to deeper ResNets and ViTs, runtime and memory measurements, component ablations, comparison with sliced Wasserstein distance, hyperparameter and feature-layer sensitivity, and qualitative diversity visualizations.

The presentation is generally clear, with explicit objectives, pseudocode, principal hyperparameters, citations for datasets and software, and a public code link. The PCBN regularizer is intuitive and empirically effective.
weaknesses: The central formulation is not convincingly novel as a Wasserstein barycenter method. Equation 5 uses one input distribution and freely optimizes the locations and weights of an m-atomic approximation. For the stated squared Euclidean cost, eliminating the free weights makes this objective exactly feature-space vector quantization/k-means: each real feature is assigned to its nearest support point and each support is updated to its assigned centroid. The paper neither acknowledges this equivalence nor compares with standard k-means, clustering, herding, or coreset targets. Moreover, Figure 2 motivates barycenters of multiple distributions, whereas the actual method uses the degenerate N=1 case.

The mathematical treatment overstates what is established. The optimal-transport value is quadratic in a support location only while the transport plan is fixed; its Hessian generally also reflects plan changes and can be nonsmooth. Thus Equation 11 is a centroid update based on the current plan, not unconditionally a classical Newton step, and the claimed convergence to a local optimum is unsupported. The supplementary bound concerns W1, while the algorithm uses squared W2, and the generic Wasserstein and MMD bounds do not show that either resulting bound is tighter.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the headline Wasserstein contribution. In Table 4, replacing CE with the Wasserstein target under PCBN improves accuracy by only 0.8-1.7 points, whereas replacing ordinary BN with PCBN accounts for gains as large as 11.3 points. There is no PCBN-only control, same-pipeline characteristic-kernel MMD baseline, uniform-weight ablation, or comparison to the equivalent k-means construction. Figure 4 instead compares different algorithmic pipelines, so it cannot support a metric-level superiority claim.

Table 1 largely combines numbers reported by other papers, while only one SRe2L setting is explicitly reproduced. The compared methods also differ in their use of a full-data teacher, FKD/soft labels, learned sample weights, and other auxiliary information; the manuscript does not account for this extra storage or fully establish identical protocols. Cross-architecture results lack uncertainty estimates, and the described 20% synthetic validation holdout is ambiguous as to whether those samples are later restored for training.

Several details needed for standalone reproduction are omitted, including barycenter initialization, the projected-subgradient learning rate and schedule, OT solver settings, handling of near-zero weights, and exactly how learned weights enter FKD and evaluation. Referring subsequent stages to SRe2L and providing code helps, but does not replace a complete specification. Efficiency is measured mainly on ImageNette at 1 IPC without a clear breakdown of teacher training, feature extraction, OT computation, relabeling, and auxiliary-data storage at ImageNet scale.

Overall, the empirical performance is promising, but the missing quantization interpretation and decisive matched controls leave the claimed Wasserstein contribution insufficiently established. These are substantive attribution and evidence issues rather than minor presentation corrections, so the balance slightly favors rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem with a simple, scalable pipeline combining class-wise feature prototypes, synthetic-image inversion, learned prototype weights, and per-class BatchNorm (PCBN) regularization.

The reported large-scale results are strong. On ImageNet-1K, WMDD obtains 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% at 10/50/100 IPC, exceeding the strongest listed results by 6.1, 4.1, and 2.8 points, respectively; similarly large gains are reported on Tiny-ImageNet.

The evaluation is broader than usual: it includes three datasets, four IPC budgets, five evaluation architectures, runtime and memory measurements, component ablations, sliced-Wasserstein comparisons, hyperparameter studies, and qualitative visualizations. PCBN produces substantial and consistent improvements in Table 4.
The presentation is generally clear, the synthetic images are visually compelling, the supplement provides implementation details and a societal-impact discussion, and public code is advertised.
weaknesses: The central conceptual contribution is overstated. With squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized support weights, Eq. 5—the best m-atom approximation under W_2^2—is exactly vector quantization/class-wise k-means: each real feature is assigned to its nearest support point and each weight is the corresponding cluster mass. The paper neither explains this equivalence nor compares against Lloyd k-means, balanced k-means, or other feature-clustering baselines. Moreover, the multi-distribution barycenter illustration in Figure 2 does not represent the singleton, support-constrained problem actually solved.

The experiments do not isolate a Wasserstein-specific benefit. Table 4 compares the proposed feature targets against cross-entropy rather than an alternative distribution metric. Figure 4 compares substantially different vanilla frameworks, provides no uncertainty, and leaves the direct MMD replacement underspecified. A controlled comparison using the same pretrained features, PCBN, inversion, and FKD pipeline with k-means, uniform weights, linear MMD, and characteristic-kernel MMD is needed; currently the gains could primarily arise from PCBN or the surrounding SRe2L-style pipeline.

Several technical arguments are inaccurate or incomplete. The claimed Hessian treats the optimal transport plan as fixed even though it changes with the support positions, so the update is an alternating/Lloyd-style step rather than an exact Newton step without additional local conditions. Algorithm 2 also updates weights after computing the transport plan but then reuses that stale plan for the position update. No convergence justification is supplied.

The appendix gives generic expected-loss bounds for W_1 and MMD, while the implemented objective uses W_2 squared. It neither verifies the Lipschitz/RKHS assumptions nor compares the uncontrolled constants, so it cannot establish superiority of Wasserstein distance. The discussion also overlooks scalable approximations to characteristic-kernel MMD.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness remain incomplete despite the code link. The manuscript omits the barycenter initialization and weight-learning rate/schedule, does not precisely explain how nonuniform weights enter FKD or downstream training, and relies on inherited SRe2L settings. Table 1 largely mixes reported baseline numbers while asserting identical settings, cross-architecture results lack repetitions or error bars, and the efficiency accounting does not clearly include every stage such as teacher training, feature extraction, and FKD. These issues make the empirical contribution promising but not yet sufficiently attributable or independently verifiable for acceptance.
